title: What is known about 1RB1LC_1LA1RF_0RD1RD_0RA0LE_1LA0LE_0RC---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_1LA1RF_0RD1RD_0RA0LE_1LA0LE_0RC---.
intro: This six-state, two-symbol Turing machine was one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project; an outside Rocq proof has since shown that it never halts when started on a blank tape. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Decided by an outside Rocq proof: it never halts. Busycoq pull request 104 (Alex Havrilla of DeepMind, 2026-11-19) proves this in Rocq, and we compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch: it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions), and its transition table is this machine. It is their proof, on busycoq's definitions of a machine and of halting, and busycoq's maintainer has not yet reviewed it. Everything else on this page is what this repository found on its own, which by itself leaves the question open.

What this repository found on its own. Four shift rules of the crossings are proved in Lean for all sizes (lean/Rules.lean); the motion of the marks and the merges were only described from simulation. The proof turns the whole run into a Collatz-like map on hub tapes: n goes to about 3n/2, in 16 phases and 32 rules (see the explainer).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 22,729 cells have been visited and 13,269 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.17·10<sup>15</sup> steps (accelerated run, blocks of 6)
claims.text: The run-length simulator tools/c/rleaccel.cpp (blocks of 6 cells, runs of a block crossed in one step, and cycle jumps, each used only after its one-cycle rule has been proved symbolically for all lengths above the minimums it needs; tested cell for cell against direct runs) runs 989,800,000 macro steps from blank tape without a halt, in 600 seconds. That is more than 1.17·1015 machine steps. It found no rule that repeats forever, so it does not decide the machine.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.1). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.493).

claims.title: Crossings of the runs
claims.text: D crosses 010 words to the right and restores them to 110; E crosses 110 words to the left writing 010, and 011 words writing 001; C crosses 001 words to the right restoring 110.

claims.title: Marks move through the runs and merge
claims.text: At the moments the tape grows on the right it reads d^x 0 0 1 1 d^y M d^z ... (d = 110, M another mark). Between such moments the mark 0 0 1 1 moves right by a fixed number of words (8 per round around step 1.2·108, with z growing by 2), so x + y stays fixed within a phase; when y reaches 0 the marks merge and a new phase starts with x small. The sum x + y at the start of a phase went 25, 44, 64, 94, 147, 196, 204, 272, 325, 425, 459, 688, 785, 993, 1203, 1409, 1899, 2073, 2507 (step 1.5·108).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape? (this repository’s own ledger)
claims.text: Not decided by the results on this page alone. It is decided outside: busycoq pull request 104 proves that it never halts (see the verdict). Before the proof: The halting transition is F1, and F is entered only from B reading a 1 (1RF), so a halt needs B> 1 1. A crossing never does that, so a halt could only come at a merge of two marks. The merges were not worked out here.

explainer.lede: It never halts. At the moments the proof watches, the tape is two long runs of the three-cell word 100, one about four times longer than the other, separated by 1010 and closed by a short end piece. One round of the machine replaces the size n of the runs by about 3n/2, and the parity of n decides which of 16 phases comes next. All 32 cases lead back into the family, so the machine runs for ever.

facts.text: No halt in the run-length accelerator (proved cycle jumps, blocks of 6).
Shift rules over runs of 3-cell words, proved for all lengths.
Length of the main run, in words, at the phase start at step 1.5·10<sup>8</sup>.
No halt in the C simulator.

sections.heading: A Collatz-like map in 16 phases that never stops
html: The proof is busycoq pull request 104 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind. We compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1, and it uses no axioms. With equivalences already recorded in busycoq, the same file settles 12 other machines that are equivalent to this one (none of them is a separate entry of the list of 608). Its core, the 16 phases and 32 rules below, is the same as in pull request 96 for 1RB1LF_0LC0RE_1LA1RD_0LB1LB_1RC1RD_0LD---, with the same step counts.

The shape of the tape. Write (100)^a for the three-cell word 100 written a times. The proof watches the machine in state A at the right end of the tape, on a blank cell. Read from left to right, the tape is then a short end piece (18 to 27 cells), then (100)^b 1010 (100)^a 1, then the head. The two counts are tied to one number n: b = 12(n + 4) + r and a = 4b + d. The small offsets r (0 to 9) and d (5 to 35) and the end piece are fixed by a phase i, one of 16. The proof calls this tape hubState i n.

One round. Write n = 2m + p, where p = 0 or 1 is the parity of n. For each phase i and each parity p the proof gives a next phase j and a small number q, from 1 to 5, such that the machine goes from hubState i (2m + p) to hubState j (3m + q), for every m. For example, phase 0 with n even goes to phase 15 with n = 3m + 1, and phase 0 with n odd goes to phase 14 with n = 3m + 3. So each round multiplies n by about 3/2, as in a Collatz map, and the parity of n picks the branch. The 32 rules cover every phase and both parities, and none of them stops. So from any tape of the family the machine reaches another one, for ever, and it never halts.

From the blank tape. The blank tape is already one of the proof's tapes, and 2,122,236 steps of the proof's fast simulator reach hubState 4 n0, where n0 is a number of 302 bits. The fast simulator stores each run as a binary number and crosses a run in one step; a second layer applies a long repeated chain of crossings at once, as a formula. Each of the 32 rules takes between 846 and 1,343 fast steps.

What is proved and what is computed. The rules for crossing runs of any length, and the formula for a repeated chain, are proved once for all lengths, and a theorem says the fast simulator only takes steps the machine really takes. To check a rule for every m at once, the computer runs the fast simulator on a tape whose run lengths are formulas s·m + t in an unknown m. A second theorem says that such a run agrees with the plain run for each value of m. The computer checks with Coq's vm_compute the way from the blank tape into the family and the 32 rules.

sections.eyebrow: Background: what the tape is made of
sections.heading: Runs of 110 and travelling marks
html:
Write d for the word 110. Each time the tape grows on the right it reads something like

d^607 0 0 1 1 d^1899 1^6 d^149 1 1 d^2 1 1 d 1^4 d^2 1 0 [A>]

(step 117,127,344): long runs of d, a mark 0 0 1 1, more marks, and the head at the right end. The head shuttles between the marks and the right end. On the way it re-encodes the runs it crosses, 110 into 010 or 011/001 and back, and these crossings are the four shift rules in lean/Rules.lean. In this example, after one round of about 2.2·105 steps the tape reads d^615 0 0 1 1 d^1891 1^6 d^151 ...: the mark has moved 8 words to the right and the run after 1^6 has gained 2.

sections.heading: Phases
html:
So within a phase x + y is fixed and the mark crosses the run at a steady rate, while the runs further right grow. When y reaches 0 the mark meets the next one, the marks merge, the runs are redistributed and a new phase starts with x small. The length x + y of the main run at the start of each phase went

25, 44, 64, 94, 147, 196, 204, 272, 325, 425, 459, 688, 785, 993, 1203, 1409, 1899, 2073, 2507 (step 1.5·108),

so the phases grow by irregular factors between about 1.04 and 1.8. The rate at which a mark moves (8 or 16 words per round in the phases looked at) and what a merge produces depend on the marks further right: a nested, Collatz-like counter.

sections.eyebrow: Background: where a halt could come from
sections.heading: Where a halt would have had to come from
html: The only halting transition is F on a 1. F is entered only from B reading a 1, so a halt needs the head in state B on 1 1. The crossings never do that, so a halt could only have come at a merge. The plan here was to list the marks, prove one round and each merge with symtm, and turn them into a map on the run lengths. The outside proof does this in its own terms: its 32 rules are such a map, and none of them reaches the halt (first section).

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.1). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.493).
After 109 steps the tape spans 22,729 cells (118 left of the start, 16,970 right), with a density of 1s of 0.584.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the round described in the proof section.

summary: Long runs of the word d = 110 with a few marks between them (0 0 1 1, 1 0 1 1, 1^6, ...). The head shuttles between the marks and the right end, and each shuttle moves a mark a few words to the right; when a mark reaches the next one they merge and the runs are redistributed, a nested counter whose phases grow irregularly. Accelerated run: no halt in 1.17e15 steps. Decided outside: busycoq PR 104 proves in Rocq that it never halts (compiled here).
